clinicalPearls: Pneumonia acquired before or during birth typically presents as respiratory distress in the first hours to days of life and often forms part of early-onset neonatal sepsis.
Infection may be acquired transplacentally, by ascending spread from the genital tract (especially with prolonged rupture of membranes or chorioamnionitis), or during passage through the birth canal.
Group B streptococcus and Escherichia coli are leading bacterial causes; other organisms include Listeria, and congenital infections such as certain viruses can also involve the lungs.
Clinical features overlap with other causes of neonatal respiratory distress, so it is often difficult to distinguish pneumonia from surfactant deficiency or transient tachypnoea on presentation.
Maternal and perinatal risk factors, particularly chorioamnionitis, prolonged membrane rupture, and maternal group B streptococcus colonisation, raise the likelihood and guide management.
Chest radiographs may show diffuse or patchy opacities, but findings can mimic respiratory distress syndrome, so imaging is supportive rather than definitive.
Because differentiating infection from non-infectious causes is difficult, empirical antibiotics covering likely organisms are usually started while cultures and the clinical course are followed.
Supportive care to maintain oxygenation, ventilation, temperature, and perfusion is essential alongside antimicrobial therapy.
reference.pathophysiology: Organisms reach the fetal or newborn lung by several routes: transplacental spread during maternal bloodstream infection, ascending colonisation of amniotic fluid after membrane rupture or with chorioamnionitis, and aspiration of infected amniotic fluid or genital secretions around delivery. Once in the alveoli, pathogens trigger an inflammatory response with exudate, impaired gas exchange, and interference with surfactant function. In early-onset disease this frequently coexists with bacteraemia and systemic sepsis, so lung involvement is often one component of a generalised infection in the vulnerable newborn.
additionalDifferentials: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
additionalInvestigations: Blood culture and full blood count with differential
Inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein
Lumbar puncture when sepsis or meningitis is suspected
Maternal history and cultures (group B streptococcus status, chorioamnionitis)
redFlags: Severe or worsening respiratory distress and rising oxygen requirement
Signs of septic shock or poor perfusion
Persistent pulmonary hypertension with labile oxygenation
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition and appropriate antibiotics and supportive care many infants recover well, but outcome depends on the organism, gestational age, and severity; fulminant early-onset sepsis with pneumonia, particularly from group B streptococcus, can be life-threatening.
pitfalls: Attributing respiratory distress solely to surfactant deficiency and delaying antibiotics in an at-risk infant
Underweighting maternal risk factors such as chorioamnionitis or prolonged membrane rupture
Relying on chest radiograph appearance to exclude infection given its overlap with other conditions
Failing to evaluate for accompanying bacteraemia or meningitis
